findings.section: §5 Text layers by format (with §1 Traceable to bytes, requirements Q1)
findings.quote: A text layer may be kept to save time, keyed by snapshot and adapter version, and is discarded when either changes.
findings.issue: The text layer is treated as a disposable cache, yet every PDF and HTML locator (a text anchor of up to 80 characters) resolves only against the output of one named adapter version. The spike found that two adapters read the same PDF differently (pdfplumber interleaved three columns, poppler did not) and that the locator window definition alone moved planted-control rejections from 6 to 5 to 3. Over a horizon running to 2030, the pinned poppler version will vanish from distributions or change behaviour.
findings.why: Extraction §1 says 'A statement whose place cannot be found again in its snapshot is not a statement.' An adapter upgrade can therefore silently turn thousands of admitted statements into non-statements. The F1 test ('the printed text at the locator supports it'), the Q1 replay and the Q8 rebuild all fail in year three with no defect in the ledger. The first real failure would surface in a published release.
findings.fix: Reverse the rule. For every snapshot that has statements, keep the text layer that produced them (under DVC, hash recorded in the statement provenance) and never discard it. Pin the adapter by a lockfile or container digest, not a version string. A new adapter version re-derives a layer beside the old one, and the locators are migrated by the reviewed old-to-new mapping of §9. Add a red test that an adapter swap cannot orphan a locator silently.

findings.section: §6.3 Assisted reading (with requirements Q5, fusion §1 and §3)
findings.quote: A proposal both readers agree on and the author does not overturn is admitted.
findings.issue: Agreement between the reader and a checker from another vendor is treated as independent corroboration. The checker examines the reader's surviving proposals, so it ratifies rather than reads independently. Vendor diversity is not training-data diversity: the spike's two judges both missed that 'Bắc' is a misprint of 'Bác', and they received no positive controls. Fusion says confidence 'falls when they disagree', which implies that agreement sustains it. The Q5 test checks only that readings come 'from more than one vendor'. The planted-item control tests recall, never checker credulity.
findings.why: Shared errors are admitted with no human look except the random sample. In Vietnamese, Indonesian and OCR-damaged text the agree-but-wrong rate is unmeasured. Those statements enter the ledger with a stance of 'agree' and high confidence. They are the statements that feed every released figure, and the error is located nowhere (Q17).
findings.fix: Add a planted-misreading control alongside the planted-item control: a row with an altered value or a transposed digit that the checker must flag. Require the author's gold sample to be drawn independently of checker stance, stratified by language and document class, and publish the measured agree-but-wrong rate with the release. Until it is measured, cap confidence for agreements at 'medium' and state that cap in fusion §3. Rewrite the Q5 test so it asserts the measured joint error rate, not a count of vendors.

findings.section: §6.3 and §5 (reader input) and collection §9 (triage reader)
findings.quote: The LLM reader is given the document's text layer, the declared scope and the declared field list
findings.issue: The documents are public and written by parties with an interest. They are fed verbatim to LLM readers and checkers, and the spec never treats them as untrusted input. Hidden text is read without distinction: §5 reads hidden spreadsheet rows and flags them, but HTML and PDF text that is invisible to a human (CSS-hidden, white-on-white, off-page, comment text) is not flagged. The locator check cannot catch an injected statement, because the injected text does exist in the bytes. The same injected instruction can steer reader and checker alike.
findings.why: A publisher or a compromised or user-generated page can plant a statement ('disbursed USD X') that the Observer records as printed by the publisher. It passes the locator check and both readers, and it violates F1's 'printed text'. It is a neutral-record failure with real attribution damage. The same exposure applies to triage at M3a, where web pages are read to decide admission.
findings.fix: Add three rules to extraction §6.3 and collection §9. (1) Readers and checkers run with no tools, no network and no file access. The document text is passed as quoted data. (2) Text adapters record visibility, and a statement whose only support is invisible text carries a 'hidden' mark and goes to the author's queue, as hidden spreadsheet rows already do. (3) The planted-item control document also carries a planted instruction that must be ignored.

findings.section: F27 Public documents only (with C6, DA9, results §7, operation §11)
findings.quote: the address at which it can be reached, or the public archive record that preserves it
findings.issue: Either a live address or an archive record satisfies F27, so the Observer's own archive capture is optional until the M4 monthly 'capture retry'. Frozen documents are 'fetched once' at M3a and not checked until M4. Redistribution is refused when terms are unknown, so the release then carries only address, hash and locator.
findings.why: A publisher can silently replace a PDF or page at the same address, or remove it, between the M3a fetch and the release. A reader who follows the address sees different content and concludes the Observer invented or misread a statement. Q8's 'independent reader reconstructs one country total' and DP-4 cannot be met for any non-redistributable document once the page has moved. The hash then proves nothing to a third party.
findings.fix: At M3a, require for every admitted document an archive capture (Internet Archive or equivalent) made at or near retrieval, with its address recorded on the retrieval. Where capture is impossible, record the reason. The release's redistribution list adds a column 'public copy exists: yes/no', and the Q8 test is stated only over documents with a public copy. Optionally, re-fetch frozen documents once just before the freeze and record any byte change as a new snapshot.

findings.section: §5 Conflicting values (with §1 Pedigree, requirements Q12)
findings.quote: Closeness to the event is the first consideration: the primary document nearest to the event carries more weight than one further from it.
findings.issue: The preference logic ranks up the party closest to the event. That party is usually the one announcing or self-reporting the money: the recipient ministry's approval headline, the donor's own pledge. Nothing distinguishes a figure stated only by the party that announces it from one confirmed by a counterparty. Nothing handles the same money being re-announced or counted by several donors. The spike already produced likely-or-better false pairings between the EU EUR 430 million package and IPG's USD 7.75 billion commitment. Independence (§1) covers mirrors and copies, not interest.
findings.why: A strategic or inflating publisher is systematically favoured. The tallies and country cards then show a self-declared headline as 'As published' with no hint that nobody else corroborates it. The marker pair 'Our calculation' and 'As published' (Q12) is silent on this, so readers will take attribution for verification. This is the main way the Observer could be quoted in support of a number that is only a press claim.
findings.fix: Derive a per-observation attribute 'stated by an interested party' from data already in the schema: the publisher's party is the funder, beneficiary or operator of the agreement or project the observation is about (via party_in and role_in). Every headline figure and country card shows it beside 'As published'. Add a check, analogous to the one on money states, that no total adds amounts announced by several donors for one programme without an occurrence or perimeter judgement.

findings.section: §7 What is redistributed (with requirements F30, C6, F23; storage §1 line-fields)
findings.quote: the statements, including their verbatim labels and short excerpts, each attributed to its publisher, document and locator.
findings.issue: Verbatim publisher text is redistributed unconditionally, while only document bytes are subject to terms. Every line-fields table ('the document's own columns, verbatim') is served, so a bulk register (the South African grants register, growing by about 3,000 lines a year) is republished whole under an open licence. F30 requires a licence with no restriction beyond attribution, which cannot cover third-party text or database content. The spec names no legal basis for holding copies (research text-and-data-mining exception, quotation right, public-sector re-use). It also has no column where terms or robots position, free registration used or public access route are recorded: retrievals and documents carry none, although C6, F27 and DA9 require them. C6 lets a single fetch 'go ahead' whatever robots rules say, while the DA9 test expects documents 'excluded by robots rules'.
findings.why: Legal exposure is the likeliest way the Observatory is taken down after launch. The release-validation step checks the redistribution list, but the data for that list and the check that every verbatim row is covered do not exist. Rungs 2 and 3 of the access ladder (session cookies, automated browser after a manual check) sit on an unstated legal assumption.
findings.fix: (1) Add a per-document terms_position value (open licence, public-sector reuse, rights reserved, unknown) plus robots and terms text hash, registration used and archive address as retrieval columns, recorded at M3a. (2) Make line-fields and verbatim labels follow the same redistribution test as bytes. Rights-reserved or unknown documents release hash, locator and a capped excerpt only. (3) State in the licence clause that the open licence covers only the Observer's own contributions. (4) Record a one-page legal-basis decision (Q21), reviewed by CNRS legal or the library, before the first automated crawl. (5) Reconcile C6 and DA9 on what 'excluded by robots rules' means.

findings.section: §3 What a statement carries and §4 What becomes a statement (with requirements N2)
findings.quote: attributed to its speaker when the publisher quotes someone
findings.issue: N2 excludes 'natural persons as signatories or delegates' only as a modelled class. Verbatim fields ('everything else the publisher printed for the item') and speaker attributions keep whatever the publisher printed: names of officials, contact emails and phones on project pages, named speakers in newsletters, and the reporter identity of any error report (F25). No rule says what is done with incidental personal data, and the ledger is committed in git and released as open data under persistent identifiers.
findings.why: Personal data of people in South Africa, Indonesia, Viet Nam, Senegal and the EU (CNRS) is published permanently in immutable releases (Results §1). That raises data-protection obligations, removal requests cannot be met, and it is out of step with the spec's own neutrality goal. It is also avoidable at almost no cost if decided before the first extraction, and painful to purge from git history afterwards.
findings.fix: Add to the declared extraction scope a default exclusion: contact details and personal names outside a published signatory or speaker position are not extracted. A speaker is recorded as an office or institution. Add a purpose-built screen (regular expressions for emails, phones and name fields, no LLM) to release validation, listing hits for the author's decision. Reports of errors store the reporter's contact outside the released tables. Add a tombstone exception to 'frozen bytes' for legal removal (see the retraction finding).

findings.section: §1 Frozen bytes, §9 Correction and restoration, §10 (with requirements F28, F29)
findings.quote:
Once published, no byte of it
is replaced, whatever is found later.
findings.issue: The only remedy for a wrong published finding is a newer release. There is no retraction or withdrawal state, no erratum shown on the wrong release's own pages, and no channel to tell outside users. Earlier releases are served only at M4 ('at M3b, the deposit of each release suffices'), so a reader landing on the old deposit or cached pages sees the wrong figure with no warning. Metadata 'papers that cite it' is entered by the author and cannot reach think tanks and journalists, who are the priority users. F28's 'even if the data must be withdrawn' has no procedure behind it. The §14 row where a book 'still reproduces from its pinned release' treats reproducing a known-wrong figure as correct.
findings.why: A finding that turns out wrong (a false match, a misread amount) keeps circulating under a valid persistent identifier. The Observer's credibility as a record that 'corrects through a channel that leaves a trace' is what the outcomes of §1 rest on. Legal or ethical withdrawal (copyright, personal data) collides with byte immutability and has no defined path.
findings.fix: Add a release status outside the frozen bytes: current, superseded by rN, or retracted (with reason). Serve an erratum file at a stable non-versioned address and set the deposit's 'obsoleted by' relation. Show a banner from that erratum on any page or deposit landing text of a superseded release (the banner is not part of the release bytes). Define a retraction tombstone: the bytes are removed, the descriptor, hash and reason remain, and the persistent identifier still resolves. Classify errors (headline-changing or not). A headline-changing error also flags the current release. Add a §14 row for each case.

findings.section: F25 Reported errors are traced (with OBS-7, OBS-5, LP-2; storage §1 adjudications; ontology §4 line classifications)
findings.quote: Each report is recorded, answered by a judgement
findings.issue: Two things the products require cannot be represented by the schema and lists as written. (1) Error reports: storage has no table for a report, its reporter, its target statement or its answer, and adjudications.decision_type is closed to 'occurrence_membership', 'flow_coverage', 'perimeter_compatibility', 'identity'. (2) A publisher's own correction, retraction or denial: fusion §2 says a judgement 'says which' (development, late report, correction), but no line classification, relation or adjudication type can carry it before the M4 attribution (F22). The classification list is closed and contains no correction notice.
findings.why: F25 and OBS-7 are M3b requirements that the storage contract cannot meet, so the test 'a report ends with a recorded judgement' fails by construction. LP-2 ('who changed official accounts') and OBS-5 need a publisher's retraction to be a first-class statement, not a value change. Without this, a published retraction is classified as a generic item and an actual correction looks like a development.
findings.fix: Add a reports table (report_id, reporter_ref held privately, target kind and id, received_at, answer adjudication, status) and a decision_type 'report'. Add a line classification 'correction_notice' and a relation 'corrects' (line to line, by the publisher), both as terms rows with definitions. Make the adjudication of a correction-versus-development judgement a typed decision (decision_type 'change_attribution') at M3b, so that F22 at M4 reads from it.

findings.section: §9 Backups and recovery (with requirements C2, N13)
findings.quote: this copy is a backup only, which no job reads, and the laptop may drop it without harm to operation.
findings.issue: The system of record for all document bytes (and therefore for F1, Q1, Q6, Q8 traceability) sits on one disk in one workstation. The DVC remote shares its NVMe partition. The only other copy is a laptop pull that the spec itself says may be dropped, made by hand after each push, and tested once at M2. The Internet Archive holds only what it captured. Zenodo holds only redistributable bytes. Documents collected through a manual browser step or behind a check exist nowhere else.
findings.why: Theft, fire, disk failure or a power event at one site destroys every non-redistributable snapshot permanently. Publishers may have rewritten or removed the originals, so the recovery rule 'refetched from its publisher' cannot restore what was said. All statements then lose their justification at once. The author is the single person who can run the recovery.
findings.fix: State that the second copy must be a different site under a different failure domain (institutional storage or an external disk kept elsewhere), not a droppable laptop pull, and that the copy is verified by hash on a schedule. Add a monthly check that the off-machine copy matches the DVC pointers. Move the test of recovery from 'once per milestone' to before each freeze and each release. Record the location and custodian of the copy in the descriptor.

findings.section: §7 Dispositions (with requirements F2, DA2, C1; operation §7.2; spike §4)
findings.quote:
A `deferred` disposition closes a document for the purpose of a run's
completeness
findings.issue: F2 passes when 'the count of documents with neither is zero', and `deferred` is a disposition. The spike projected 58 to 210 author hours of review for the 115 pending documents, against a proposed budget of 3 hours a week: 19 to 70 weeks (derived from those two figures). Every author-only act (admit, accept a milestone, freeze, cut a release, publish) also stops if the author is unavailable. Nothing states what a reader sees then.
findings.why: M2 can be declared complete, with F2 and DA2 green, while most of the 115 documents are deferred. A single overloaded or absent author becomes the single point of failure of the whole horizon to 2030. A release would continue to say 'maintained' while nothing moves.
findings.fix: Add to M2 acceptance a stated ceiling for deferred documents (a share, by document class) and require the list to be named in the acceptance. Add a dormancy rule: each release's descriptor and every Observatory page state the last accepted release date and whether maintenance is active, so that an abrupt stop is visible. Record in operation which author-only acts an agent may prepare completely so that a successor could sign them.

findings.section: §7.1 The measurements and §5 Where each reader runs (with extraction §1 Declared method, Q4, Q9)
findings.quote: Prices move; the run records the actual cost.
findings.issue: The design names specific LLMs and prices (frontier, mid and economy tiers), and the spike itself hit model churn (a model id that returned HTTP 429, three provider failures in 33 calls). The local LLM is a shared service the Observer cannot reconfigure. The coding agents depend on the author's subscriptions, which §4 excludes from spend. Extraction §1 requires a method change to have 'its effect on earlier output … reviewed', but for an LLM reader the spike shows the effect is large (57/59 kept against 13/46 from a field-list change alone). Nothing says what happens when a reader or checker is retired, repriced or replaced between M2 (this year) and M3b or M4, or when the coding-agent vendor changes terms.
findings.why: A replacement reader silently changes statement counts and classification rates between the documents read at M2 and those read later, with no result flagged as mixed. A price or model change can also stop a run mid-campaign with no sanctioned fallback ('never switches vendor'). The maintenance model of Q18 and Q19 depends on one coding-agent vendor.
findings.fix: Add a reader-substitution rule to operation §5. A new reader or checker LLM is a new method version and is admitted only after it passes the planted-item and planted-misreading controls and reproduces the author-checked statements (the Q17 set) at a stated minimum agreement. Every release lists which LLM version read which documents. Re-derive budgets from run reports, not from listed prices. Name the fallback when the coding-agent vendor is unavailable (the fast test tier and the specification must be runnable by any agent).

findings.section: §7 The secondary-to-primary pass (traceability rate)
findings.quote:
The share of claims examined that are traced
(held, admitted or unreachable)
findings.issue: The traceability rate counts 'traced, unreachable' (a primary document is identified but cannot be fetched) as traced. Nobody has read that document, so nobody has verified that it carries the claim. The identification can rest on the tracker's own citation, and trackers are the sources most likely to be wrong, strategic or recycled from each other.
findings.why: The published M3a traceability rate (a headline figure in Q10 and DP-1) overstates how much of the trackers' quantitative content is supported by a primary document, and it does so most where the primary is hidden. A reviewer cannot tell from the number which claims were actually checked.
findings.fix: Report three numbers instead of one: share traced to a document actually read (held or admitted), share traced to an unreachable document, and share untraced or secondary only. Drop 'unreachable' from the numerator of the headline rate, or label it explicitly as 'identified, unread'.

findings.section: 1. Tables and rules (tables `lines`, `line-referents`, `observations`); with extraction 3 and 6.3; requirements Q4, Q9, Q17
findings.quote: country, sha256, locator, ordinal, label, classification, own_status, own_status_axis, own_sector, groups, recorded_at, notes
findings.issue: The provenance the prose promises has no table to live in. The `lines` row has no method, method version, run, reader, checker stance or author decision, although extraction 3 says every statement carries them and F1, Q4, Q9 and Q17 are M2 requirements. No table holds individual reader and checker outputs (Q17: 'every machine reading ... is kept'), rejected proposals ('recorded with its reason, never dropped'), extraction dispositions (extraction 7), or collection's triage judgements. The decision table `line-referents` has one `confidence` column where fusion 3 requires stance, likelihood, confidence, a quoted basis and the readers' answers. Provenance is also scattered over per-table `method`/`decided_by` columns, and none of them holds what makes an LLM reading replayable: the dated model version, the routed provider, the prompt hash, the sampling settings and the raw response.
findings.why: In W3C PROV-O terms (Entity, Activity, Agent, plan), the spec models entities and agents but has no Activity. Without a run record, an auditor cannot say which agent with which plan generated a line from which snapshot and text layer. This is the thing F1, Q4, Q9, Q15 (spend per run) and Q17 (errors located at a step) need, and it is the thing the planned PROV-O export needs to be mechanical. The spike's claim that 'Model, prompt version, temperature and adapter recorded' holds only because the prototype wrote its own logs. Provider aliases change silently (and the spike routed through OpenRouter and saw provider failures and retries), so a bare LLM identifier is not a version. Storage is marked 'in force' and its DDL is about to be written, so the gap will be baked in.
findings.fix: Add a PROV-shaped core before the DDL. (1) A `runs` table, one row per extraction, reading or judgement run: run_id, kind, agent (person, script, or LLM id with its dated or pinned version and routed provider), plan (method, method_version, prompt hash, sampling settings), started_at, ended_at, inputs (snapshot sha256 and text-layer adapter version), spend and author minutes (this makes Q15 computable). (2) `run_id` on `lines`, `observations`, `line-referents`, `relations`, `adjudications`, dispositions and triage rows, replacing the ad hoc method columns. (3) A `readings` table, one row per reader or checker output (proposal, stance, likelihood, confidence, quoted basis, raw response hash), plus a `dispositions` table and a triage-judgement table, each naming the step at fault when a human decision rejects a reading. (4) Raw request and response bytes stored under their hash, as the reproducibility record. Map Retrieval to prov:Activity, Snapshot to prov:Entity, run to prov:Activity, and record the mapping in `terms.external_scheme`, so that the later RDF export is a view.

findings.section: 6.3 Assisted reading of one-off documents (and 14 Open questions, 3 Text of F-level acceptance)
findings.quote: A proposal both readers agree on and the author does not overturn is admitted.
findings.issue: Agreement between two LLMs is used as the admission rule, but the spec never says what the audit sample is for. It fixes no estimator, no acceptance criterion and no published accuracy figure. The sample is drawn only from the agreed proposals (a precision audit). Recall rests on the checker's 'missed' list, which is another LLM reading the same text. The spike shows how weak that list is: 22 of 28 'missed' items were the pipeline's own rejections, and some duplicated kept rows. The sample size is left open in section 14.
findings.why: (a) Agreement is not accuracy. LLMs from different vendors agree on wrong answers far more often than chance, and more so within a model family (Kim, Garg, Peng and Garg, 'Correlated Errors in Large Language Models', ICML 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.07962). LLM judges also show self-preference and position bias (Zheng et al. 2023, MT-Bench). Operation counts a Qwen model served by another company as Alibaba, but distilled families are still correlated. A rule that admits unreviewed agreed rows needs a measured defect rate, or the ledger's 'checked' label is an assertion. (b) The random sample is exactly what lets you measure precision with a bound: 0 errors in 59 audited rows bounds the defect rate below 5% at 95% (rule of three). Not stating this leaves the author reviewing sample rows as a ritual while the release carries no accuracy claim. Data-quality frameworks (ISO 25012, ISO 8000) name accuracy and completeness as core dimensions, and the release's validation and coverage reports have neither for D2. (c) A reader's and a checker's misses are correlated, so capture-recapture between them (the Chapman estimator) overstates recall. The standard unbiased method is to audit a random sample of the source text, not of the output.
findings.fix: State in 6.3 that the author's decisions on the sample are a labelled audit set that produces two published numbers per document class: the precision of admitted rows (Clopper-Pearson or Wilson interval, stratified agreed/disagreed) and the recall within declared scope (a random sample of scope passages, about 30 per class, checked by the author for unextracted assertions). Add a reopen rule: if the lower bound of precision or recall falls below a threshold declared per class, the class's agreed stratum is reviewed in full or the run is deferred. Replace the open question by a method rule: draw n to meet a target interval width with a floor of 3 (sample sizes stay method, not requirement). Add the two figures to the release's validation report and to Q5's test. Drop the word 'kappa' unless it is computed: agreement statistics such as Cohen's kappa are unstable at the extreme prevalence of this task (Feinstein and Cicchetti 1990), so report raw precision and recall with intervals.

findings.section: 1 Principles (Calibrated language) and 3 (The judgement; Reading and verification)
findings.quote: a stance (the same, different, or undetermined), its likelihood and confidence on the calibrated scales
findings.issue: The IPCC terms are applied to machine output without any calibration step, and the record is ambiguous. (1) Nothing tests whether an LLM's 'likely' or 'very likely' means 66-100% or 90-100% empirically. The spike shows 2 of 7 pairings were false at 'likely' or above, and the judges said 'same, very likely, high' on a match whose tier-2 string overlap was 2 tokens in 10. (2) A stance plus a likelihood double-encodes one quantity: 'different, very likely' equals 'same, very unlikely'. It also collides with the spec's own 'about as likely as not, very low confidence' for a judgement that knows nothing, versus the stance 'undetermined'. It is unclear whether 'likely or more' is applied to the stance or to 'same'. (3) 'Confidence' is defined as evidence quality plus 'agreement between readers'. In the IPCC guidance (Mastrandrea et al. 2010) confidence rests on evidence and agreement in the literature, and is reported separately from likelihood. Here it becomes a derived scalar from two or three LLM outputs, and the threshold is a conjunction of two ordinal scales with no stated order.
findings.why: Verbalised LLM confidence is systematically overconfident (Xiong et al., ICLR 2024, https://openreview.net/forum?id=gjeQKFxFpZ). The match threshold is the knob that decides every published count (F11), so an uncalibrated 'likely' silently sets the published figures. A reviewer cannot check a threshold whose terms have no empirical meaning. Two implementers will read stance and likelihood differently.
findings.milestone: M3b (the checker's stance and terms appear at M2 and triage at M3a, so the rule must be fixed before M2)
findings.fix: (1) Define one quantity: the likelihood that the candidate is the same (or that the proposal is right); drop 'stance' as a judged value and keep 'undetermined' only as a recorded abstention or disposition. (2) Publish, per method version, a calibration table on the hand-judged set (the 257 register rows and 67 plan lines already matched by hand, plus the author's audit decisions): the observed precision for each verbal term, with its interval, and a reliability check. Use the observed rate, not the nominal IPCC range, when a threshold is translated into an expected error. Require the method version to name the table. (3) Define the threshold as an ordered rule (the likelihood term first, confidence as a separate filter) and state it once in fusion 1; say that confidence from agreement between readers is a method statistic, not IPCC evidence confidence, and name it differently (for example `reader_agreement`).

findings.section: 3. Two match thresholds
findings.quote: The two figures are the low and the high end of the result's range.
findings.issue: Matching more does not move every figure the same way. A project count or an agreement sum falls when more candidates merge (the inclusive threshold gives the lower figure), while a perimeter membership or coverage figure rises. The sentence fixes the order wrong for referent counts and sums. Two thresholds out of a continuum, applied to pairwise links that chain into clusters, give a sensitivity band, not a bound, and nothing shows the two ends bracket the figure at intermediate thresholds.
findings.why: The published 'range' would be read as an interval on the true value, as a confidence interval is. It is a two-point sensitivity analysis under method choices (and, given point 3 of the calibration finding, under uncalibrated terms). NUSAP and the IPCC guidance both say to state what an interval means. Check 3 of section 14 ('differs between the inclusive and the cautious threshold') leaves the direction open, so an implementer cannot fail it.
findings.fix: Say 'the cautious and the inclusive figure; the range is their minimum and maximum, and is a sensitivity range to the declared thresholds, not a probability interval'. Compute the figure at the declared grid (cautious, inclusive and one intermediate point) and report min and max, or assert monotonicity per result kind. Label the range in the Observatory 'sensitivity to matching' rather than uncertainty.

findings.section: 3 Identity (A candidate match; Proposers) with storage 3 and 4
findings.quote: Every judgement about identity is a judgement on a candidate match, and each candidate match has its own chain of judgements.
findings.issue: The matching design is pairwise only, with no cluster semantics, and it reinvents Fellegi-Sunter without its named parts. (1) Referents are clusters, but judgements are pairs. The spec never says what a referent is when A~B and B~C are accepted and A~C is rejected, or how connected components are formed at a threshold. Single-link chaining at the inclusive threshold is a known failure: project counts can collapse. Storage 3 assumes 'a `same_as` cluster that the design bounds to depth one' without a rule that enforces it. (2) The tiers are a cascade of blocking plus comparison (tokens compared 'within a country and a technology group'), and the cautious and inclusive thresholds are the two-threshold match, possible-match, non-match region of Fellegi-Sunter (JASA 1969), unnamed. It has no blocking recall, no m/u-style evidence weighting, and no pair or cluster evaluation metric beyond 'tested against matches already judged by hand'. (3) Tier 2 is string-token based, and the spike shows it fails across languages (overlap of 2 tokens in 10 for the Bac Ai pair). Exact identifiers are 'virtually certain', yet extraction 3 admits that printed numbers have 'gaps, repeats, restarts', and plan ordinals and operator codes are reused.
findings.why: Known failure modes of record linkage (transitive closure violations, blocking that never proposes the true pair, identifier reuse) are not guarded. The count of projects at M3b, the headline published figure, depends on them. Naming the established structure lets the builder use known methods and metrics instead of inventing them.
findings.fix: Add to section 3: (a) the referent at a threshold is the connected components of accepted pairs, and a transitivity violation (A~B, B~C, A not~C at the same threshold) is raised as a conflict for review, never silently merged; (b) state that tiers 1-3 are blocking plus comparison, name the cautious/inclusive pair as the possible-match band, and require a blocking-recall figure (what share of hand-judged true pairs the proposers surface at all, per language pair); (c) evaluate on the hand-judged set with pairwise precision and recall and one cluster metric (B-cubed or cluster F1), published with the method version; (d) for key-based pairing, require a corroborating attribute (same country, near-equal amount or capacity) before 'virtually certain', or downgrade to 'very likely'; (e) block tier 3 and 4 candidates on typed attributes (place, capacity, operator) rather than label tokens when the labels are in different languages.

findings.section: 1. Tables and rules (as-of rule, decision tables); fusion 8
findings.quote: An as-of state at cutoff K is the set of rows with `recorded_at` on or before K that are in force under the supersession rule.
findings.issue: This sentence states the bitemporal as-of rule wrongly. 'In force' is defined on the whole chain (terminal and accepted). Applying it first and then filtering by `recorded_at` removes a row that was in force at K but superseded after K, and excludes the terminal row if it was recorded after K, so neither row stands at K. Fusion 8 states it correctly ('Take each chain of judgements to its state at K'). The decision tables also do not carry the field the rule keys on: `line-referents` and `relations` list `decided_at`, not `recorded_at`, while the rule says 'every decision table carries `recorded_at`'.
findings.why: F10 and the release's central promise ('a later discovery never changes what an earlier result said') depend on this rule. The established bitemporal model (Snodgrass; SQL:2011 system-versioned tables) needs a transaction interval per row: start (`recorded_at`) and end (the `recorded_at` of the superseding row). A filter on start alone gives wrong answers as soon as the first supersession occurs after a cutoff. The error would surface only after M2 has written supersession rows, and M2 is where as-of is tagged. `decided_at` (the world time a person or program decided) and `recorded_at` (ledger time) are also conflated, so a judgement decided in July and written in October would count at a July cutoff.
findings.fix: Rewrite the rule: a row is in the as-of state at K when `recorded_at` <= K and it has no successor with `recorded_at` <= K; then apply the status test to the chain as it stood at K (a revoked chain at K revokes). Add `recorded_at` to `line-referents` and `relations` and state that `decided_at` is descriptive only. Add a check to fusion 9 and a test to the DDL: a chain A, then B superseding A after K must return A at K. Also state that valid time lives in `timings` only.

findings.section: 6. Known items and the recall estimate
findings.quote: If that search channel is missing from the frame, the frame is revised (a recorded revision) and the new search channel is searched like the others.
findings.issue: The known-item list is both the held-out test set and the diagnostic instrument that edits the search frame at each checkpoint. After a missed item leads to a new channel, the same item (and its neighbours) can be found by that channel and then counts as found in the final recall. Round-zero holdings also count ('admitted or held from round zero'), although they were assembled by the author from the same academic and grey literature that supplies the known items.
findings.why: This is adaptive reuse of a test set, which biases the recall estimate upward beyond the visibility bias the section already admits. The Wilson interval '36 of 40, 90% (77 to 96%)' would be published as the gate for M3b, and it is the stopping rule's third condition (at least 90%). The interval assumes the items were not used to tune the search. The stopping rule's point-estimate test on n=40 is also a coin-flip around the threshold: the lower bound is 77% at exactly 90%.
findings.fix: Split the frozen list before round one into a development part (used at checkpoints for diagnosis, may trigger frame revisions) and a held-out part (opened once at the end, never used to revise). Publish recall on the held-out part only; publish the development-part result as a diagnostic. Count an item that triggered a frame revision as missed in the final estimate. State how many of the round-zero holdings derive from the literature that built the list, and report recall with and without them. Make the stopping condition on recall use the lower interval bound or state explicitly that it is a point-estimate gate.

findings.section: 3 Documents (proposers) and extraction 2 (Language extracted in a translation pair)
findings.quote: Agreement of title, publisher, publication date, page count and any identifier the document prints: a partner's mirror and, with language detection, a translation.
findings.issue: In IFLA LRM terms a translation is a different expression of the work, and an abridged, updated or summarised English version is another expression again. The spec treats `translation_of` as 'the same publication in another language' and then extracts from one member only ('from one language of a translation pair'), leaving the other citable but unread. The only evidence for the pair is metadata agreement (title, date, page count), which is weak across languages and does not show that the two members carry the same statements. No check compares content.
findings.why: A known failure mode in multilingual collections: the English version of a Vietnamese decision or plan is often an abridgement, a draft or a later revision, with a different annex or updated numbers. Folding it into the canonical member drops statements silently. The spec's own rule that a dropped member 'remains citable' then points readers at a document with statements that are not in the ledger. The defect would reach the corpus (DA5, F3) and hit the four-language design at M2.
findings.fix: Before folding a translation pair, compare language-independent content: the multiset of numerals with units, dates, percentages and named identifiers printed in each member (plus table counts and page structure). Record the result with the `translation_of` judgement. If the fingerprints agree, fold as now. If they differ beyond a declared tolerance, do not fold: keep both as documents related by a weaker relation (for example `related_expression`), extract the differing parts from each, or extract both and let fusion see them as two statements by the same publisher. Add a case to extraction 15.

findings.section: 2 Document and 3 Relations (`edition_of`); collection 10; language (table of retired terms)
findings.quote: each issue found is its own document, linked by `edition_of`
findings.issue: `edition_of` names three different relations: a revised version of a work (an amended plan), an issue of a serial (a newsletter, a quarterly report), and the version history of a living page. The third is already a snapshot, not a document. Ontology 2 says an edition is 'a document row related to its predecessor'; the language document says edition means 'a publisher's successive issue'. The spike found that an issue is not an edition and that restatement and pairing are defined only for snapshots of one document (0 of 7 restatements between issues 8 and 13). Storage 4 calls the Indonesian plan-to-progress-report link an 'edition relation' although a plan and a progress report are different kinds of document.
findings.why: LRM and serials practice (ISSN, continuing resources) treat an issue as a part of a serial aggregate, and a revised edition as a new expression of the work. Web archiving (Memento, RFC 7089) treats versions of a living page as time-indexed captures of one resource. Mixing them means the M2 parsers will write `edition_of` rows that later code has to split, the restatement check will run between issues where it is meaningless, and Observatory pages will show 'editions' that are not.
findings.fix: Split the relation before M2 rows are written: `issue_of` (document to series, carrying stated periodicity, used for collection's series class), `revision_of` (a later expression of the same work, distinct document), and no relation for living-page versions (they are snapshots of one document, keyed by retrieval time, as in Memento). Reserve `edition_of` or drop it. Restatement and unpaired-absence rules apply between snapshots of one document and between `revision_of` members; between issues, pairing is a candidate match judged under fusion 3 with the author seeing every pair at M2, as the spike proposes. Rename the Indonesian CIPP-to-progress relation (for example `reports_on`).

findings.section: 1 Principles (Pedigree; Independence of publishers)
findings.quote: Each statement carries a qualitative assessment of where it comes from, in the sense of the NUSAP pedigree
findings.issue: Pedigree and independence are principles with no data home and no rule. No storage column or table holds a pedigree, and results (results 2) carry none. NUSAP pedigree (Funtowicz and Ravetz 1990; van der Sluijs et al. 2005) is an ordinal matrix: each criterion is scored on a defined scale (typically 0 to 4) with rubric anchors, so that two assessors score the same way. Here the four dimensions are listed but have no scale or anchors. 'Independence' requires detecting copying between sources, which is an open problem in truth discovery (Dong, Berti-Equille, Srivastava 2009), and the only mechanism offered is a `cites` relation at M3b. No result reports how many independent supports a figure has.
findings.why: A rule that nothing implements and nothing can check will be built, if at all, as an unreviewed heuristic and then displayed to readers as though it were evidence quality. It also contradicts requirement C8 (build only what an M2 or M3 requirement needs) and the author's rule that every rule serves a checkable need. Pedigree is also the one mechanism that could justify 'closeness to the event' as a weight in section 5.
findings.fix: Either cut pedigree and independence to 'M4 or later' with no M3b text, or make them derived and checkable. Derived version: pedigree is computed, never judged, from existing columns. Proximity from `authority_category` and the party's role, production from `document_type`, entry from extraction method, and independence as a graph computed from `same_as`, `translation_of`, `cites` and shared-publisher edges, reported as a count of independent supports per figure. Define a four-step ordinal rubric per criterion as `terms` rows and store the derived pedigree in `data/derived`. Say that copying undetected by these edges is not excluded.

findings.section: 5 Ontology tables (`status-crosswalk`, `sector-crosswalk`, `terms`) and Traceability
findings.quote: *(publisher_id, own_status)*, axis, shared_status, recorded_at, decided_by, status, supersedes, notes
findings.issue: The crosswalk rows are SKOS mappings but carry no mapping strength. The Traceability paragraph requires SKOS `mapping_relation` for terms taken from external vocabularies, and says 'Similar labels do not justify `exactMatch`', but neither crosswalk table has a `mapping_relation` column. So `D. Completed` to `closed` and `implementation` to `implementation` are stored alike. Also, `terms` holds classes and relations as well as values (`kind`), and the planned 'SKOS export' covers all of them, though SKOS models concepts in concept schemes, not classes and properties (RDFS/OWL). The table has no `broader` column, so no hierarchy is expressible even where the sources have one (for example IATI and CRS purpose code families).
findings.why: Published counts by shared status (F14) mix exact and broad mappings unless the weakest mapping used travels with the figure. SKOS `exactMatch` is transitive and means interchangeable, so an invalid one leaks into every derived count. A generated SKOS export of relations and classes would be invalid or misleading for any consumer that harvests it, which is the FAIR I2 argument for exporting at all.
findings.fix: Add `mapping_relation` (the five SKOS values) to both crosswalk tables and require it at acceptance. Have the results metadata state the weakest mapping used for each shared-status or sector figure (or a cautious and an inclusive mapping set, like thresholds). Add a nullable `broader_term_id` to `terms`. Restrict the SKOS export to `kind = value` lists (one ConceptScheme per `list`) and export classes and relations as RDFS properties or not at all.

findings.section: 5 How a release is built; 6 Persistent identifier and Metadata
findings.quote: every file of the package, with its relative path, byte size, SHA-256 hash and immutable address
findings.issue: The descriptor reinvents an established manifest (Frictionless Data Package, RO-Crate, BagIt) and leaves its format open, as with the 'data dictionary' and the 'metadata record in a standard, harvestable schema'. The spec also has a bootstrapping loop it only partly solves: the descriptor records 'the persistent identifier' and the deposit records the release identifier, yet a DOI normally exists only after deposit, and the descriptor is hashed before it.
findings.why: F29 and F31 tests ('every field appears in the dictionary') are checkable only if the dictionary is machine-readable, such as a Frictionless Table Schema with foreign keys generated from the DDL, or CSVW metadata. A standard package format (RO-Crate is JSON-LD with schema.org and can carry the run record) gives FAIR interoperability and reuse (I1, R1.3) and machine validation at no cost. Without a named standard, each implementer builds a private descriptor and F29 becomes uncheckable.
findings.fix: Name the formats: `datapackage.json` (Frictionless) or an RO-Crate for the descriptor, Table Schema generated from the DDL for the dictionary, DataCite metadata schema for the deposit record, with relation types `IsNewVersionOf`, `IsPreviousVersionOf` and `IsSupplementTo` for the release chain and code. Say that the persistent identifier is reserved before the build (repositories such as Zenodo allow this) so the descriptor can name it, or that it appears only in the deposit metadata and never in the hashed package.

findings.section: 6.3 Assisted reading of one-off documents (with jetp-operation.md 7.2 and 13; spike-REPORT.md 4)
findings.quote: the items the checker says were missed, and a random sample of the proposals they agree on
findings.issue: The review rule has no bound on total author minutes. Every disagreement and every missed item goes to the author, and the sample share is open (extraction 14). The spike projects 7,000 to 12,000 proposals and 58 to 210 author hours for the 115 pending documents. At the operation budget of 3 hours a week that is 19 to 70 weeks for M2 alone. Missed items are the largest share, and 22 of the 28 missed items on decision 1009 (v3) were the pipeline's own locator rejections. The scope and field-list approval per document is not counted at all.
findings.why: Author attention is the binding constraint (C1). As written, M2 cannot be accepted in reasonable time. The only escape is mass deferral, which makes the M2 claim of 'every document extracted' vacuous. Money is not the constraint: USD 14 to 26 of model spend against tens of hours of author time, so cheap extra machine layers are nearly free.
findings.fix: Replace 6.3's author step with a bounded, checkable rule. (1) Mechanical filters cost no author minutes: a rejected locator goes back to the reader once for repair; the missed list is de-duplicated against proposals and rejections; a missed item counts only if the checker's quoted span resolves by the locator check and lies inside the declared scope. (2) A third reader from a third vendor, economy tier, is called on disagreements only. Two of three decide and all three stances are recorded; only a three-way split or low confidence reaches the author. (3) The author queue is capped per document, for example 10 items sorted by confidence then materiality (amounts, counts, statuses before headings and furniture). That is 15 min a document, a ceiling of about 29 h for 115 documents, derived from the spike's 1.5 min per item and expected at about half. Items beyond the cap are not admitted; they stay pending or the part is deferred. (4) Replace the proportional random sample with a fixed-size audit sample per document class, for example 30 agreed rows per class, drawn with a committed seed. Publish the error rate with its Wilson interval, as collection 6 does for recall. If the upper bound exceeds the declared tolerance, revise the class template and rerun; do not review more rows. About 8 classes x 30 rows x 0.5 min is 2 h. (5) Scope and field list are fixed once per document class or series, approved once, and only exceptions are logged. This closes open question 14. The 3-reader panel is a narrowing of the M4 panel, not the full one.

findings.section: 7.2 Proposed amounts and 8 Review minutes
findings.quote: 100 items presented (disagreements, missed items and random sample together)
findings.issue: The budget is counted in items at an assumed 30 seconds. The spike's rule gives 1.5 min per disagreement or missed item and 0.5 min per sampled row. So 100 items is 50 to 150 min, not 50. There is no total for a milestone, only per run and per week. Per-run caps with deferral let the total grow without bound across 14 to 40 runs.
findings.why: A cap in the wrong unit is not a cap. The author cannot tell in advance whether a sitting fits one evening.
findings.fix: State author budgets in minutes per sitting, per week and per milestone, and price each item class (disagreement, missed, audit row, scope or template approval) at its measured or spike rate until logged sittings replace it. Add an M2 attention ledger: total hours spent and remaining, reported in every run report. A run whose queue would exceed the sitting budget splits by document, not by asking for more minutes. Reconcile with the proposed per-document cap in the review-rule finding.

findings.section: 1 Tables and rules (with jetp-extraction.md 3, 6.3, 7, 9)
findings.quote: country, sha256, locator, ordinal, label, classification, own_status, own_status_axis, own_sector, groups, recorded_at, notes
findings.issue: The M2 schema cannot hold what extraction requires. `lines` has no method, method_version, reader, checker stance, likelihood, confidence or decided_by. It has no status or supersedes, although extraction 9 says a misread statement is superseded. No table holds dispositions (extraction 7), proposals and rejected proposals with reasons (6.3), per-call cost (Q17), or the step at fault. `line-field-specs` is per document, while the spike shows it must be per class or series.
findings.why: Q4, Q17, F2 and F5 are M2 tests and cannot pass without these records. The pending list is 'snapshots with neither statements nor a disposition', and the disposition has nowhere to live. This is the largest unbuilt piece of the M2 slice, and the slice does not size it.
findings.fix: Add to the M2 tables: `dispositions` (snapshot or document, kind, reason, decided_by, method, method_version, recorded_at, supersedes, status); `readings` (reading_id, run_id, snapshot sha256, locator, proposed label, reader LLM, prompt version, checker LLM, stance, likelihood, confidence, basis, tie-break stance, author decision, step at fault, rejected reason, cost, tokens); and `runs`. Add method, method_version, decided_by, status and supersedes to `lines`. Decide where `readings` lives given the file ceiling, for example DVC-tracked JSONL per run, with the admitted line carrying the reading_id and a hash. Change `line-field-specs` to key on document class or series with per-document exceptions.

findings.section: Q1, Q4, Q17 and DA2
findings.quote: The pipeline reproduces the statements of the 254 documents already extracted, byte for byte, or every difference is explained.
findings.issue: 13,089 statements from 253 snapshots already exist, produced before this specification. The requirements and extraction 3 demand method, version, checking reader and author decision on every statement, and replay 'by the current pipeline'. The spec never says how many of the 13,089 come from parsers, LLM reading or hand, nor what legacy rows carry in the new columns. Replay binds only parsers (extraction 10), so the reach of Q1 is unknown.
findings.why: Without a rule for legacy rows, M2 acceptance (zero unexplained differences, Q4 'every statement extracted by an LLM names its LLM') is either unreachable or silently waived. Porting old parsers into the new pipeline is probably the biggest M2 build item, and it is not sized.
findings.fix: Add an M2 rule: pre-specification statements carry method `legacy` with a recorded version or commit, are exempt from checker-stance fields, and are listed in the replay report by method. State the count per method (parser, assisted, hand) for the 13,089 and name the parsers to be ported. Q1's test reads 'zero unexplained differences for statements whose method is a parser, and a locator-and-text check for the rest'.

findings.section: 5 Where each reader runs; 7.1; 13 Open questions
findings.quote: Local Qwen3.8-27B on padme, when the part fits its context and a pilot shows its readings pass the checker at a rate the author accepts
findings.issue: The M2 slice includes a local-LLM bulk-reader pilot, yet money is not binding. The spike projects USD 14 to 26 for all 115 pending documents with hosted mid or economy readers, and measured USD 0.03 to 0.08 per document. The operation budget instead derives USD 42 to 55 for a full pass over all 278 held objects, but M2 reads only the 115 pending, since the 254 extracted are replayed without an LLM. A local reader would save about USD 10 and cost GPU days on a shared service. The spike did not use the local model, and 7,000 to 12,000 statements at about 285 output tokens each is 2 to 3.4 million output tokens, with unmeasured long-document throughput. It adds a second method family to calibrate and keep, for little gain. The per-run 'USD 60 for the full M2 pass' rests on the wrong population.
findings.why: This is an M2 scope item with no M2 requirement behind it, apart from C3 'local compute first', which the money numbers do not justify. It also puts a cross-vendor rule (Alibaba reader, other-vendor checker) into the M2 test matrix.
findings.fix: Default M2 readers to paid hosted LLMs from two vendors plus the tie-break vendor. Move the local-LLM bulk-reader pilot to M4 or to 'when volume exceeds the monthly cap'. Re-derive 7.1 and the per-run budget on the 115 pending documents and the spike's measured costs, at about USD 15 to 30 with a margin for chunking and repair passes. Soften C3's test to 'each reading method names where it runs'.

findings.section: 6.2 and 6.3 (large and bulk documents), with jetp-operation.md 5
findings.quote: A document longer than the reader's context is split into parts with their own scope, as extraction § 6.3 provides
findings.issue: Extraction 6.3 says only 'split into parts with their own scope, or deferred'. It gives no chunk rule. Twelve of the 115 documents exceed 100,000 characters, and the ZAF plan is 304 pages. A 32k output cap allows about 110 statements per call. Nothing says how parts are cut, whether they overlap, how an item that straddles a part boundary is handled, what window the checker sees, or how the missed-item list is scoped per part. The spike's two JavaScript portal bundles hold 5.0 million characters, about half of all pending text, and their route (structured read, shell verdict or LLM) is not fixed by a size or structure rule.
findings.why: Without it, the biggest documents either blow the per-document budget and the author queue or produce duplicate or truncated statements. A 2.5 million character bundle sent to an LLM would be a large, avoidable cost and review load.
findings.fix: Add a short M2 chunk rule: cut at declared scope parts (section or page ranges), with a fixed overlap; one locator per item, so the (sha256, locator) uniqueness check deduplicates overlaps; the checker reads the same window plus its neighbours; missed items are scoped to the window; each part has its own queue and cap. Add a size and route gate to 6.2: a snapshot above N characters is first probed deterministically (structure, embedded literal, shell) and only a verdict 'prose in scope' admits LLM reading; bulk bundles are never LLM-read in full.

findings.section: 4 The repository as control plane, Gates
findings.quote: A change is reviewed by an LLM of another family than the one that wrote it (requirement Q19), and the review's findings are answered on the pull request before merge.
findings.issue: Run outputs are 'changes like any other', each with cross-vendor LLM review plus a full `make check` on padme. M2 produces 115 documents' statements, dispositions and reports. Per-document or per-batch PRs each get the full review loop, which the project's own notes price at tens of minutes and about 1M tokens per gated PR. A row-level LLM review of a data PR duplicates the 6.3 checker and is not meaningful at 10,000 rows.
findings.why: The gate cost multiplies with the number of PRs and competes with the author's review time. It also gives false assurance: the real row check is the 6.3 queue, not the PR diff.
findings.fix: Distinguish code PRs from run-output PRs. For a run-output PR the gate is the mechanical validator, the planted-item and fabricated-locator controls, replay and idempotence on the run, and the run report. One cross-vendor review reads the report and a sampled trail, not the rows. Batch by run, not by document. The rows themselves are reviewed through the 6.3 queue.

findings.section: 1 Tables and rules (file ceiling) and 3 Engine
findings.quote: Lines of hand-read documents stay per-document files reviewed row by row in a pull request.
findings.issue: Three problems. (1) The 512,000-byte ceiling and the country-year shard rule cover tables, but `line-fields/<document_id>` has no shard rule, and a long document or bulk bundle will exceed the ceiling, so the pre-commit hook will reject it. (2) Row-by-row diff review cannot hold at 7,000 to 12,000 new rows, and it contradicts the 6.3 queue as the real review. (3) Sizes disagree: 'about 8 000 rows today' in storage 3 against 13,089 statements in requirements DA2. So the ceiling arithmetic, which runs to tens of shards and thousands of rows a year, is unverified.
findings.why: The writer has to implement sharding for per-document field files at M2, or the first large document fails at commit time. The review claim misleads the gate design.
findings.fix: Extend chunking to `line-fields`: `<document_id>.d/NN.csv` at the ceiling, joined in order like the other tables. Say that assisted-reading output is reviewed through the 6.3 queue and the run report, and only bulk and parser output through a manifest diff. Reconcile the row counts, and give a per-year byte estimate for lines, line-fields and readings against the ceiling.

findings.section: 5 Text layers by format
findings.quote: A text layer may be kept to save time, keyed by snapshot and adapter version, and is discarded when either changes.
findings.issue: Every locator is defined against a text layer produced by a 'named adapter version', and the spike ran poppler 24.02.0, a system binary. An OS upgrade or a different machine changes text order and, per the spike, pdfplumber against poppler already decides whether statements exist. The spec does not say where the text layer is stored, whether the adapter is pinned in the repository, or what happens to 13,089 plus new locators when the adapter moves. The fast tier on doudou has no adapter.
findings.why: Locator resolution is the traceability oracle (F1, Q1). If it silently depends on a system package, replay and the release's provenance decay before the 2030 horizon (C10). This is a cheap decision now and an expensive incident later.
findings.fix: Decide once: either pin the adapter in the repository lock (a locked Python wheel, not apt poppler) and test locator resolution against it in the slow tier, or store the text layer of each snapshot behind an admitted statement as a DVC artifact of record, keyed by (sha256, adapter version). Name its location (DVC, not git), and state that the fast tier does not resolve locators.

findings.section: 7.2 Reaching a budget and 10 Service failures
findings.quote: A run never switches vendor to stay under a vendor budget without the author's agreement
findings.issue: The spike saw 3 provider failures in 33 calls (about 9 %) and an HTTP 429 from one vendor, and had to substitute another model mid-run. The spec retries three times, then leaves the document pending, and forbids any switch without the author. An unattended overnight run stalls on the first vendor outage and waits for the author's attention.
findings.why: The author is the only human and batches decisions; a stall per outage turns into the very interruption C1 tries to avoid. Reader and checker substitutions are also real method changes, which the ledger must record.
findings.fix: Have each run header declare, in the author's single pre-run decision round, an ordered fallback list per role (reader, checker, tie-break) with the constraint 'checker's family differs from reader's', enforced by the harness. A switch inside the list is automatic, is recorded per call, and starts a new method version tag on the affected rows. A switch outside the list stops the run as partial. A vendor monthly cap pauses only that vendor's role.

findings.section: 8 Dated snapshots and restatements (with spike-REPORT.md 5, point 3)
findings.quote: [M2 for key-based pairing; M4 for pairing without a key across the periodic collection]
findings.issue: Stored restatement links, 'unpaired' records and change detection are tagged M2. No M2 or M3 step produces a second snapshot of a held document: M2 does no discovery, M3a fetches once, and living-document refetch is M4. Restatement has no storage column or table (the ledger's line `same_as` is a different relation). The spike also proposes moving key-less pairing of serial issues into M2 with the author seeing every pair. No M2 or M3 requirement needs it: F22 and OBS-5 (change between releases) are M4. The spike found 0 of 7 pairs to be restatements and 2 of 7 false at 'likely'.
findings.why: This adds build and author load to M2 for an M4 consumer, and a bad pairing is worse than none. Collection 10's `edition_of` for series also conflicts with the spike's `issue_of` finding.
findings.fix: M2 keeps only the pipeline properties: identical bytes share a snapshot; new bytes are extracted in full, append-only; F4's test runs on a fixture. Restatement stays a derived query over keyed parser output, not a stored link. Stored restatement, unpaired and change records, and any key-less or serial pairing, move to the first refetch at M4. Reject the spike's move of serial pairing to M2. Add only the `issue_of` relation (replacing `edition_of` for series) so the 13 MOIT issues are independent documents.

findings.section: 4 Matching records, Scope of the first implementation (with jetp-fusion.md 3 Documents; jetp-collection.md 2)
findings.quote: tiers 1 and 2 at collection time, so a snapshot whose text already exists is registered as a `same_as` candidate before extraction; tier 3 as a candidate generator over the registered documents. [M3b for lines; M2 for documents]
findings.issue: Document de-duplication is tagged inconsistently. Fusion 3 lists proposers 1 to 5 for documents (including an LLM reading of first pages and a person) as M2. Storage 4 limits M2 to tiers 1 and 2 plus a candidate generator. Collection 2 tags 'duplicates are settled before anything is extracted' as M3a. Operation 5 puts identity judgements at M3b. Extraction 2 and F3 need it at M2.
findings.why: M2 must fold mirrors before extraction, or statements and counts double. But the LLM tiers need the reader, checker and author loop and add to the queue, and the pending list depends on the outcome. An implementer cannot tell what to build.
findings.fix: State one tagging. M2: tiers 1 and 2 (identical bytes; normalised text) deterministically, plus the tier-3 candidate list shown to the author as a bounded pair queue (for example at most 30 pairs, sorted by likelihood). M3a: tier 4, the LLM reading with the 6.3 checker, when discovery brings mirrors (collection 9 already makes duplicate a triage outcome). Retag collection 2 and fusion 3 to match.

findings.section: 2 What a result carries (with jetp-fusion.md 7 and jetp-ledger-storage.md 1)
findings.quote: The kinds of result the M3b release must contain are those the requirements name
findings.issue: The same sentence lists 'accounts (fusion § 7)'. No requirement names accounts: section 4.4 is only a heading, F14 needs states selected not added, and F19 needs the gaps between states. Yet fusion 7 Reconstruction (opening, disjoint cover, closing, residual), the Markers coefficient account, the `marker-coefficients` and `deflators` tables, and the `flow_coverage` adjudication roles `opening` and `closing` are all tagged M3b. The presentation adds an accounts page, 'Money'.
findings.why: This is C8's own test failing: rules tagged M3 that cite no M3 requirement. It is also the most expensive machinery in M3b (exact cutoffs, coverage judgements, residuals) and needs yet more judgements from the author.
findings.fix: Retag Reconstruction, Markers, `deflators`, `marker-coefficients` and the coverage roles to M4 or later. M3b results are counts by unit and scope (F13), sums selecting one financial state (F14), rate-cited conversions (F15), gaps between states (F19) and excerpts (F21). Strike 'accounts' from the M3b result kinds in results 2 and presentation 'Money' until a requirement asks.

findings.section: 11 Reading statements into observations, Methods (with jetp-fusion.md 3)
findings.quote: a checker from another vendor on every observation, the author on the disagreements and a random sample
findings.issue: The D3 reading and the D4 matching queues at M3b have no size, yet they repeat the M2 attention problem. Roughly 13,089 plus 7,000 to 12,000 statements give tens of thousands of observations, each with its own reader, checker and author sample. Fusion 3 says 'every candidate match gets a judgement' against about 8,000 CRS rows and 1,301 IATI lines. The spike shows tier 2 fails across languages, so most matches fall to LLM tiers. Operation budgets cover per-run minutes, not the M3b total.
findings.why: M3b is also gated by author minutes, and the spike only measured extraction. Without a bound, M3b inherits a 50 to 200 hour queue at least as large as M2's.
findings.fix: Apply the same bounded rule (mechanical filters, tie-break reader, per-item cap, audit sample per class) to reading and matching, with an M3b attention ledger. Scope the work: read observations only for statements in the strict JETP scope that feed a declared result; headings and out-of-scope classes yield none; prefer deterministic reading rules per series. Match only lines that feed a result, with blocking by country, technology and capacity, and a top-k of candidates per line. Report unjudged candidates as 'listed, not counted' under the F11 threshold rule.

findings.section: Organisation and vocabulary; Page top: two bars (and absent M3b slices in fusion, storage, presentation)
findings.quote: Click, tap, Enter and Space toggle it; ArrowDown opens it on its first link; Escape and a click outside close it.
findings.issue: Results and extraction state an M3b slice. Fusion, storage, presentation and the requirements' milestone table do not, and the whole presentation document is tagged M3b, including dropdown key handling, the country chip, breadcrumbs, folded 'About this page' text and word-for-word copy rules. M3b also carries F16 to F18 and F20 (timelines, funding roles, transition functions, asset joins) alongside F11, F12 and F19. The 'M3b slice' is therefore not minimal, and the requirement tests F20 (four asset cases) and F18 are each a judgement project of their own.
findings.why: The author's rule is 'something that works first, then M4 polishes'. An unbounded M3b delays the first citable release, which is the point of the milestone. Since the site is already built, the tags mislead rather than gate.
findings.fix: Add an 'M3b slice' section to fusion, storage and presentation. Presentation: one page per served table (F23), the two number markers (Q12), the release banner and trail links; keyboard and dropdown behaviour, chip, breadcrumbs, folds and plain-language glossary move to M4. Propose an explicit build order inside M3b: release 1 is documentary counts by unit with tier-1 matching; F11 and F19 joins follow; F16 to F18 and F20 only as far as the author confirms, otherwise M4.

findings.section: 7.2 Proposed amounts (with jetp-collection.md 6, 7, 9)
findings.quote: Judgement: no measurement in the repository
findings.issue: M3a effort is not bounded. Every candidate gets an LLM reader, a checker and author sampling, yet the candidate volume is unknown (88 OpenAlex queries, four countries, several languages, eight search channel classes, plus a web-search budget of USD 25 with no measure). The secondary-to-primary pass needs at least three recorded searches per claim, with no sample size declared before the protocol. The known-item list needs at least 40 items authored outside the frame.
findings.why: The stopping rule and the recall estimate are only as cheap as the candidate volume. The author's triage queue can balloon exactly as in M2, and the USD 25 cap may fire before the frame is covered.
findings.fix: Add deterministic pre-filters before any LLM triage (normalised URL and hash match against the register, domain and language filters, dedupe against round zero). Give the triage queue a per-round minute cap. Fix the trace-pass sample size in the protocol (for example 100 claims, drawn with a committed seed). Replace the USD 25 'judgement' by a measured cost per search from a one-country pilot round before the campaign is declared.

findings.section: Q14, Q15, DA6, C8 (with extraction 6.4 and DA4)
findings.quote: Test: every design rule tagged M2 or M3 cites a requirement of that milestone.
findings.issue: Milestone tags disagree or cannot be audited. Q14 is M3a and M4, while operation 1, 8 and 10 tag 'one run, one report' and final states M2 for extraction runs. Q15 is M3b, yet operation 8 tags review-minute logging M2 and cites Q15, so by C8's test an M2 rule cites an M3b requirement. DA6 records a document class at M3a, which needs a checked judgement per document and has no M3 consumer, and the `documents` table has no class column. Extraction 6.4 builds transcription at M2, while DA4 accepts a disposition that names the format, and the spike found one scan in the 115 pending. Most extraction, fusion, storage and operation rules carry no requirement id, so C8 cannot be checked.
findings.why: A reviewer cannot say whether the M2 slice is minimal, and implementers may build M4 items early.
findings.fix: Retag Q14 to M2 for extraction runs, and Q15 to 'M2 record, M3b state'. Record the document class at M4 except the `series` flag needed for parser selection. Retag transcription by method to 'M2 for the `deferred` disposition and the person's direct reading; OCR and recogniser pipeline when a scan is in scope'. Add requirement ids to every M2 and M3 bracket (for example [M2; Q4]), and move any M2 rule that cites none to M4.

findings.section: 1. Tables and rules (lines table), against jetp-extraction.md 3, 6.3 and jetp-requirements.md F1, Q4, Q17
findings.quote: country, sha256, locator, ordinal, label, classification, own_status, own_status_axis, own_sector, groups, recorded_at, notes
findings.issue: The D2 schema has nowhere to keep what extraction and Q17 require. `lines` has no method, method_version, extraction run, checker stance or author decision. No table holds machine readings (reader proposals, checker stances, prompt versions, cost, tokens) or rejected proposals. Extraction 6.3 says a rejected proposal is "recorded with its reason, never dropped", and Q17 says a rejection "names the step at fault". No table or column receives either.
findings.why: F1, Q4, Q9 and Q17 cannot be met by the schema as written. AEDIST's whole use of the Observer (AED-2 accuracy per reading, AED-3 cost per method, AED-4 processing change against document change) depends on readings being rows. Adding them after M2 means rewriting the writer and re-deriving provenance for the 254 documents already extracted. Nothing said later in the horizon (new readers, new vendors, re-reads after model retirement) can be recorded without it.
findings.fix: Before the writer is coded, add to D2 (a) `lines.method`, `method_version`, `run_id`, and (b) a `readings` table keyed by proposal: snapshot sha256, run_id, role (reader, checker, person), LLM id and version, prompt version, sampling settings, stance, likelihood, confidence, quoted basis, tokens, cost_usd, proposed locator, outcome (locator_rejected, admitted, rejected), rejected_step (retrieval, extraction, reading, matching), decided_by, line_id (null when never admitted). Validator rule: an admitted line has at least one reader row and, for assisted reading, one checker row. Name the table in F23 as served or not served.

findings.section: 6.2 Q17 and 3.7 AEDIST (with jetp-extraction.md 6.3)
findings.quote: thus serve as reference answers for research on machine
findings.issue: The claimed reference answers are produced by the readers that AEDIST will benchmark, and are checked by a human only on disagreements, missed items and a random sample. Extraction 6.3 admits every row both LLMs agree on and the author does not overturn, so most of the set has never been seen by a human. Recall cannot be measured at all, since an item both LLMs skip is never listed (the spike found 6-8 missed per 3-page issue, some of it scope creep). AEDIST states it measures "recall, precision, cost and latency". The spec defines no gold subset, does not record how the sample was drawn, and the release contents (Results 4) omit readings and decisions altogether.
findings.why: Used as reference answers, the set rewards models that resemble the Observer's own reader and checker, so accuracy is inflated and recall is unmeasurable. The AEDIST reuse, and the data-paper claim of located errors (DP-2), would then rest on a circular set. Flags that were not recorded at admission cannot be reconstructed later.
findings.fix: State in Q17 which subset is a reference set. (1) Record per admitted statement a verification class: author-decided, in the random verification sample (seed and inclusion probability recorded), or machine-agreed only. (2) Before any machine run, hand-read a small gold set per document class (scanned decision, prose news, series PDF, HTML page, spreadsheet) and flag it gold. Recall is reported on the gold set only. (3) AED-2 accuracy is computed on gold plus sample, never on machine-agreed rows. (4) Add the readings table and the verification class to the release (Results 4) so AEDIST can cite a versioned reference set. (5) Record that the Observer's reader and checker LLMs are also candidate AEDIST benchmark LLMs.

findings.section: 8. Dated snapshots and restatements
findings.quote: snapshot, which is extracted in full, as if for the first time, under the same
findings.issue: The only no-op test is byte identity, but the spec itself knows that living web pages change bytes without changing content (Fusion 3 proposer 2: "a web page whose timestamp changes on every" visit). Every changed-bytes retrieval is therefore extracted in full (LLM reader, checker, author queue). Every unchanged item then becomes a new line row linked to its earlier twin, with pairing without a key left to M4. The linking shape is unstated: chain or star. Storage 3 bounds `same_as` clusters to depth one, and a chain of 156 weekly restatements breaks that bound. Counts of "statements" (F13) would count each restatement again. `line-fields/<document_id>` has no chunking rule against the 512,000-byte file ceiling.
findings.why: Derived, with the number of living documents N not stated in the spec: measured mean 13,089 lines / 253 snapshots = about 52 lines per snapshot; weekly for three years is about 2,700 restatement rows per living document per year, about 108,000 a year at an illustrative N=40. Storage 3 sizes the design for "tens of thousands of lines a year". The LLM and author cost of re-extracting unchanged prose weekly is the larger problem (spike: USD 0.03-0.08 and 12-21 review items per clean pass). DA11's claim "no change of design" fails, and the line shape must be fixed at M2 because F4 is an M2 requirement.
findings.fix: (1) Add a content-equivalence step before extraction: compare the declared-scope normalised text layer of the new snapshot with the last extracted one. Equal means a persistence record (retrieval to snapshot, no new lines, no LLM call). (2) When they differ, extract only the changed regions for parsers, and for assisted reading re-read only the changed passages, with restatement judged per typed value (spike finding 3). (3) Store persistence as a thin row (line_id, retrieval_id), not a new line, and link any restated line to the first origin line (star, depth one). (4) State that a statement count counts origin lines, with restatements a separate unit. (5) Add a chunking rule for `line-fields/<document_id>`.

findings.section: 5. DA11 Expected volume (with jetp-operation.md 7.2 and spike-REPORT 4)
findings.quote: with no change of design
